content:
Oh yeah, that's a very common misconception outside of the nonbinary community about the use of transition labels! I'm happy to explain. 

First off, the transmasc/transfem labels have evolved over time. They started gaining traction in the early 2000s — although they had existed since at least the '90s — and were used as a catch-all term for anyone who was trans, without having to necessarily identify as transsexual or binary transgender. Like many historical labels, they have existed for most of their history as nebulous terms with no set definition, just a general vibe.

To start, I want to note that some of the earlier attempts at defining those labels did try to describe them in terms of what one is transitioning away from, instead of what one's actual gender identity is.

For example, 

advocate S. Leigh Thompson (who is a trans man) proposed this definition in 2006

: 

Transmasculine: Any person who was assigned female at birth but feels that is an incomplete or incorrect description of their gender.

That being said, those sorts of definitions never really became the predominant ones inside of nonbinary communities. And as of right now, they are actively disliked by most. For one, they don't take into account intersex people, who might have a complex history with gender and might use "contradictory" labels like AFAB transfem or AMAB transmasc. Furthermore, those definitions just.. don't make sense from a nonbinary perspective. Which is a big problem, since the labels transfem/transmasc are supposed to be used to include (some of) us.

Those definitions stem from the exorsexist idea that there is only one possible direction of transition: away from your "biological sex" and towards the "opposite sex". But gender is more complex than a line that goes from "man" to "woman" in which getting away from "man" necessarily pushes you towards "woman" and vice versa. For example, a medically-transitioning transneutral person might wish to remove their gendered characteristics (breasts, facial hair, etc.), but not wish to gain the ones associated with the opposite sex, like a binary-aligned trans person typically would. Even though they are transitioning away from typical presentations of their assigned sex-gender, their transition is also atypical for transfems/transmascs norms, and categorizing them as either of those just based on their AGAB would be reductive. Not to mention that social transition (being recognized as one's actual gender by society) is an integral part of transitioning, too. Categorizing a trans person as transmasc or transfem when they don't consider their gender identity masculine nor feminine is basically misgendering. At the end of the day, you (general you) are still telling someone who sees themselves as neutral, or androgynous, or fluid, or anything else they might identity as, that they need to be categorized based on the gender binary.

This framework also leads to the false idea that nonbinary people will always have more in common with binary trans people of the same "biological sex" than a nonbinary person of the "opposite" one with a similar gender identity. This is simply not the case, and in nonbinary spaces we rarely divide ourselves based on AGAB. A transmasculine or transfeminine enban might feel understood and included in trans man/woman spaces, but that's because they are transitioning towards masculinity/femininity just like them, not because AGAB inherently creates a connection between trans people. I, for one, feel a lot more understood amongst other neutral/unaligned people than I do around more binary-aligned people with my same AGAB.

Now, there are people who, despite being told all of this, will still argue in favor of using the labels in the way you (asker) have observed from others. Often under the guise of "society at large is transphobic and doesn't recognize nonbinary genders, so your oppression can only be described accurately if the labels indicate what you're transitioning away from". And my question to them is: if society is transphobic and doesn't recognize me as my actual gender, shouldn't a trans advocacy movement strive to change that, instead of telling trans people their identity doesn't exist? Furthermore: why does transness always need to be defined in terms of suffering? Why should an identity label be assigned to me based on how society (mis)treats me, instead of giving me the agency to choose the words to describe my own experience?

And, if you allow me to be petty for a second, the trans people arguing for using transfem and transmasc in that way are exhibiting a real "rules for thee but not for me" attitude. Because if someone said "trans women and trans men are not recognized as their actual genders by society at large, so we're going to use these labels that actively misgender them to describe their transition" they would, rightfully, lose their minds. But when it comes to nonbinary people, it's suddenly fine to force us in gendered categories that don't match our actual gender, based entirely on our AGAB. It's a double standard, and antithetical to what trans advocacy should stand for. 

At the end of the day, enben deserve to have words to describe our transition without forcibly binarizing us and our experiences. This is why we have labels such as transneutral and transandrogynous, and sometimes I wonder if more people would identify with them if they were more widely known and widely accepted.

Our identities and our language shouldn't revolve around what bigots think of us. To circle back to the example you brought up: an unaligned nonbinary person should be able to say "I'm unaligned and I've faced a lot of transmisogyny in my life" and be taken seriously, without their identity being called into question, without having to disclose their AGAB to "prove it", and without having to adopt the transfem label (if it doesn't resonate with them) just to be included. Unfortunately, as it currently is, a lot of us feel like we have to binarize our identity in order to receive solidarity.

I hope this explains it, and I'm glad you brought up the topic, anon! I have been meaning to talk about this for a while.

… I don’t care?

title: #…oh #how do I stop?
content:
queeranarchism

:

pine-branches

:

caspercryptid

:

I feel like not enough people realize that people under enormous strain act really really fucking Weird 

things humans are known to do when stressed:

-hallucinate

-cry over what seems to be small things

-become furiously angry over what seems to be small things

-hit a self destruct button over and over again

-lose all sense of reality

-becoming straight up unable to communicate

-view every situation as life or death

-experience delusions/become vulnerable to irrational worldviews

-perceive hostility where none exists

-become extremely nauseous and/or throw up

-stop engaging in sleeping/eating/basic hygiene

-stop processing sensory input

-process way too much sensory input all at once

-lash out at others/themselves

-and more!

being able to recognize when a human (ie. you or another person) is so stressed out they cannot think clearly is VERY important for conflict resolution and diffusing emotional crisis. highly recommend trying to train yourself at being able to recognize that state of panic- there is a point in which logic and rationality is useless and you have to address the underlying emotional issue first. knowing that saves everyone a lot of pain and struggle.

It’s also good to understand that all of these reactions are USEFUL. They’re all part of our survival system, telling us we need to be able to fight better, flight better, freeze better, fawn better. 

-hallucinate > some experiences are too difficult for our brain to process all at once. To avoid complete overwhelm, the mind seeks distraction and escape or translates invisible stress into visble metaphors. 

-cry over what seems to be small things > Crying releases tension. Our body needs it. If we don’t cry over the Big Stress, we will cry over the small things to regulate.

-become furiously angry over what seems to be small things > Rage also releases tension. Our body needs it. If we don’t rage over the Big Stress, we will rage over the small things to regulate.

-hit a self destruct button over and over again > Our survival instinct does not accept powerlessness. When we lose all sense of control over reality, we do whatever makes us feel in control again. If the only control we can have is self-destructive, that is the control we will reach for.

-lose all sense of reality > again, some experiences are too difficult for our brain to process all at once. To avoid complete overwhelm, the mind seeks distraction and escape or translates invisible stress into visible metaphors. 

-becoming straight up unable to communicate > Too much stress is really bad for us, not just mentally but also for our heart, our blood pressure, our digestion, etc. Our biology has a fail safe system: if the stress is too much, shut parts of the brain down. Block the input until the stress is lowered, so that at least we don’t overload complete.y 

-view every situation as life or death > When we go into survival mode, our body is pumped full of stress hormones and they linger (both because your body needs time to process them and because we’ve evolved around predators that might linger in an area, so we’ve evolved to stay on guard long after a danger). Our body keeps us in survival mode - ready to fight/flight/freeze/fawn to keep us alive. 

-experience delusions/become vulnerable to irrational worldviews > again, some experiences are too difficult for our brain to process all at once. To avoid complete overwhelm, the mind seeks distraction and escape or translates invisible stress into visble metaphors. 

-perceive hostility where none exists > again, when we go into survival more we stay there a while - ready to fight/flight/freeze/fawn to keep us alive. 

-become extremely nauseous and/or throw up > when we go into survival mode, our body puts all its energy into the organs that we need to fight/flight/freeze/fawn. Digestion is suppressed. It can wait. (This is also why stress constipation is a thing). If what’s currently in the stomach can not stay there and wait, best to get rid of it so the body doesn’t waste vital energy on digestion. 

-stop engaging in sleeping/eating/basic hygiene > Again, when we go into survival mode, our body is pumped full of stress hormones and they linger. They keep us awake. They suppress feelings of hunger, thirst etc. to make us better survivors in the moment of danger. 

-stop processing sensory input > again,  if the stress is too much, our system shuts parts of the brain down. Block the input until the stress is lowered, so that at least we don’t overload completely. 

-process way too much sensory input all at once > part of that survival mode again, this is here to keep us safe

-lash out at others/themselves> part of that survival mode again, 

-and more!

These are all processes designed to keep us alive, to keep us safe. Experiencing them isn’t just normal, it’s useful. We would be much worse off if our body-brain-system didn’t have all these safety valves to regulate us during and after experiences that are too intense to process without such safety valves. Yay to all our useful weirdness! 




#…oh #how do I stop?

Good question! Since all of these are 

some form of ‘stuck in survival mode’, and 

functional 

Trying to stop the behavior generally does not work and is likely to make things worse, because suppressing survival mode mechanisms tends to just give you more stress. 

The only real answer

 

is:

 reduce the causes of stress

Depending on your situation, that can be very difficult, but it’s the only way to really get out of constant survival mode. 

Next: 

give your body some recovery. 

Sleep, food, warmth. Plenty of it. 

And 

give your brain some stability

. Routines, traditions, familiar places, family recipes, showers. Things that push your 'i feel safe here’ buttons. 

When you are feeling a little less constantly in danger, next steps:

Connect to the world around you. 

Have dinner with friends. Take a walk outside. Touch grass. Hug a dog. Talk to someone you love. 

Connect to your sense of control and capableness.

 Stress feels helpless and out of control, so do small things that do the opposite: fix a flat tire, learn a new song on your guitar, complete a puzzle. 

Connect to your sense of meaning

. Stress can make everything feel pointless. Connect to what gives your life meaning. Is it friends? family? social justice? religion? great sex? It’s your life, there are no wrong answers here. You don’t have to do any meaningful things for now, the point is to rediscover what motivates you. 

Finally:

Take your time. 

It takes a long time to get your survival mode to switch off. Recovering from a short period of very high stress generally takes about 6 weeks. Recovering from a long, intense period of stress can take much longer. Recovering from a full burn out can take years. Don’t give up just because you experience a relapse. Notice whether the waves of bad things are getting less bad over time. 

Work through guilt and shame. 

Guilt and shame will keep you back in survival mode, as will any believe that you do not deserve to feel better. If you notice these things in your head, tackle them. You responded to stress the way all humans do. Your behavior was not weak, weird, broken, etc. Your survival mode was doing what it’s supposed to do. As long as you’re still here, it worked.

If you want to actually help trans people, employ us so we can fucking survive. Hire us and train us. Fucking help us live.

title: Forget Flock. Now The Cameras Can Read Your Pockets Too.
content:
Forget Flock. Now The Cameras Can Read Your Pockets Too.

: 

reading-writing-revolution

:




We’ve spent a lot of time here on surveillance you at least perceive in some way: the camera on a pole; the reader in the car; the thing you can photograph, complain about at a council meeting, and occasionally get banned. License plate readers have been the headline act for years now: a camera sees your car, logs your numberplate, files it in a database, and a network of them quietly reconstructs where you’ve been.

A defence contractor called Leonardo has decided that reading your plate is no longer enough. Their new system, ELSAG SignalTrace, reads everything else you’re carrying.

You drive past a sensor, and it doesn’t just photograph the car. Instead, it grabs the wireless signals leaking out of every device inside it: your phone, your smartwatch, your earbuds, your fitness tracker, the car’s own Bluetooth, tyre pressure sensors, the key fob, and in some cases, even your pet’s microchip.

Then it ties all of that to your numberplate and stores these data for later.

It is, as far as branding goes, refreshingly honest. The product page’s own subheading is “Identify Suspects by the Electronic Devices They Use.”

Confident; they’re not even trying to hide it.

 so clearly we recognize that there is a worse position to be in. content:

Can all the anti-capitalists stop reblogging this noble savage bullshit and start connecting with the material reality of human well-being. There is no one way humans were ‘meant’ to live and this just stereotypes all pre-historical cultures into one hippy caricature. 

But also, like quite a lot of anarchists: I’ve done most of this shit. I’ve lived in communities that camped in nature and cooked around a fire together and sang and danced and told each other about cool edible plants. 

It certainly had some benefits for my mental health. It didn’t fix systematic oppression, it didn’t protect me from transphobia, it didn’t solve that I did’t have access to health care. Systemic problems require systemic solutions. 

Having tried the community-in-nature life and being able to compare it to 'individualist’ 21st century life, I can say that access to a hot showed, heating, a bed that supports my back, a nutritionally balanced diet and medication also have pretty huge benefits for my mental health. Maybe, Idk… redistributing the fruits of our society according to everyone’s needs. That would be pretty good for our mental health.

[“In a world that constantly shames us for our bodies, genders, or sexualities, we can trick ourselves into thinking that we are “taking control” and that achieving a certain body ideal is liberation. It is far from that. 

For those of us who face multiple forms of oppression, developing eating disorders is not simply wanting our bodies to meet the impossible aesthetic ideal associated with people in dominant culture. Queer and trans people don’t develop disordered eating simply because we want to assimilate to cisgender, heteronormative culture. Of course, appearances can be and often are part of the picture. But when we attribute eating disorders solely to the desire for our bodies to look a certain way, the conversation stops. And we miss out on opportunities for crucial conversations about the connections between eating disorders, trauma, and survival.

Eating disorders help us to survive trauma and oppression.

Eating disorders help us to cope with everyday microaggressions and macroaggressions. They help us to get by in the face of food insecurity. They can keep us safe in a world in which being read as queer or trans can mean life or death.
